Off-topic and please don't let me derail this thread (if this turns into a longer discussion then we can perhaps move it): Is there a way of tracking how many PRs have needed to be merged before one can state this one IMO problem idiomatically? I think it's absolutely commendable that the community are doing this properly (and would expect nothing less from Joseph) but it's also interesting to see how much formalization one IMO problem has motivated.

The statement of the problem can be seen here https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/2024_IMO_Problems/Problem_4 . It is a standard 2d geometry problem about a triangle, involving the incircle, circumcircle and some tangent lines. IIRC this is the problem which DeepMind's bespoke tool (not their Lean tool, their geometry tool) solved in about ten seconds flat. This thread is perhaps an indication of why they didn't try their Lean tool on it!

We've been able to state this one for a long time, most of the PRs are for proving it. It's a bit fuzzy whether the PRs initially setting up definitions of inspheres and tangency should be considered as part of the PRs towards (stating and proving) this problem, or just as generally setting up definitions to support stating more past IMO geometry problems, but if they are then it's a bit over 100 in total (even without those I think it ends up as about 100 PRs for the solution).

For stating other IMO geometry problems, some of the most frequently encountered gaps in mathlib include polygons (we have an active PR, though definitions for convex polygons will need building on top of that), arcs of circles (we also have a recent PR), areas (recent Zulip discussion, no PR from that yet) and some kind of bundled definition of an angle bisector as an affine subspace (line) (older Zulip discussion on how to set that up doesn't seem to have resulted in a PR).

The main thing I'd push on is the affine-span-restriction boilerplate. The same preamble

let S : AffineSubspace ℝ P := affineSpan ℝ (Set.range t.points)
let t' : Triangle ℝ S := t.restrict S le_rfl
have hf2 : Fact (finrank ℝ S.direction = 2) := ⟨by ...⟩
have : Module.Oriented ℝ S.direction (Fin 2) := ⟨...⟩

shows up four times in #32282 and once in #32294, and there are already two copies in Angle/Sphere.lean and Sphere/Power.lean. I'd prefer to factor out:

namespace Affine.Triangle

scoped instance (t : Triangle ℝ P) :
    Fact (finrank ℝ (affineSpan ℝ (Set.range t.points)).direction = 2) :=
  ⟨by rw [direction_affineSpan, t.independent.finrank_vectorSpan]; simp⟩

noncomputable scoped instance (t : Triangle ℝ P) :
    Module.Oriented ℝ (affineSpan ℝ (Set.range t.points)).direction (Fin 2) :=
  ⟨Basis.orientation (finBasisOfFinrankEq _ _ Fact.out)⟩

noncomputable def spanRestrict (t : Triangle ℝ P) :
    Triangle ℝ (affineSpan ℝ (Set.range t.points)) :=
  t.restrict _ le_rfl

end Affine.Triangle

Each call site is then just simpa [spanRestrict, ← AffineSubspace.angle_coe] reduction plus the actual oriented application. scoped keeps the instances out of global typeclass search, which feels right given the orientation is an arbitrary choice.

Separately, the _aux lemma in #32294 is ~150 lines; the affine-independence sub-proof and the isosceles A = X branch could reasonably be lifted to named lemmas.

I've opened #39696 with versions of the first two scoped instances (for general simplices, and for any finite-dimensional space in a Module.Oriented.Arbitrary namespace, respectively). As noted there I don't see why the simplex instance is only found by typeclass search at one of the two use sites. And I'm more dubious of spanRestrict given that adding one definition would mean adding lots of API about how it interacts with all other definitions relating to simplices so any uses of that extra definition may not be worth the cost (note that we don't yet have the full set of such API for map or restrict, though I believe we do for reindex).
Note that #31892 (no comments, a non-reviewer approval three weeks ago) does not involve any of these issues.

I've also now split out the affine-independence sub-proof in #32294. Given that each such proof split out involves quite a bit of boilerplate for readability (using let to define notation A, B, C, I, X for points and stating a series of trivial facts about them such as A_mem), this made the file 25 lines longer, and given that the isosceles case is quite short, I haven't split it out. I'm leaving off the refactoring of #32282 and #32294 in terms of instances in #39696 until the latter PR is merged into master, rather than adding an extra dependency to #32282 and #32294 before then.
Note incidentally it's taken nearly six months to get this far (#32295 was opened on 30 Nov 2025 and there are still seven open PRs in this series).

I don't think the auto-assignment system really works well. It has the properties (a) assignments can be freely ignored, and mostly are, rather than any expectation that people either accept and act on or reject an assignment, and (b) a PR is only auto-assigned to one person at a time. But if it's essentially notifying people that a PR might be of interest to them, which (a) implies, then (b) (together with a long interval before a PR gets unassigned / reassigned) doesn't make much sense, and auto-assignment might make something less likely rather than more likely to be reviewed.

Also, some of the PRs have had review comments that have been acted on / responded to - but from people who aren't reviewers, so don't have "maintainer merge" rights, so it's not clear how much such a review helps progress things towards inclusion.

(An implicit question there is: who is most actively reviewing mathlib PRs - in any topic - without being a reviewer, and should such people be made reviewers if their reviews are showing good judgement?)
